prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock, in which neutral atoms confined at a magic wavelength are interrogated in large numbers, and for its development to a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18, opening new tests of fundamental physics and relativistic geodesy

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B012 alone, Katori and Ye. After the full exchange the case is, if anything, easier to state. The scientific step is one idea with a testable consequence: at the magic wavelength the light shifts of the two clock states cancel, so many atoms can be held without Doppler or recoil shifts and a very narrow transition read out with the statistics of an ensemble. That idea is distinct from the frequency comb (2005), which measures optical frequencies, and from single-ion control (2012), which relies on one ion and its quantum-limited signal. The result has been reproduced and surpassed in several laboratories and species, so its validity does not depend on the credited names. The two names correspond to two identifiable contributions, the concept and first realisation (Katori) and the route to record accuracy and comparison (Ye). I treat the seven-to-one split in round 1 as a reason to test the argument harder, not as evidence; the argument survived the tests I could apply.
statement.case_against: The attribution reservation remains. Takamoto, Hong, Ludlow, Lemke and the PTB, SYRTE and NIST groups made decisive contributions that two names do not cover, and I cannot verify from the files in front of me who first demonstrated the strontium versus the ytterbium lattice clock. The pending redefinition of the second leaves part of the payoff prospective. Eriksson's point that a conceptual reorganisation of a field (B030) is, as a kind of achievement, closer to what many would call a discovery is not answered by anything in the clock case, and I accept that the choice between the two is partly a matter of the committee's reading of the statutes rather than of fact. I also have to admit that my own expertise is far from precision metrology, so I rely on the specialists' agreement about the physics and cannot independently check the lineage claims.

responses.point: Eriksson maintains B030 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) as his sole preferred part as the most defensible conceptual discovery within condensed matter, ranks B012 eighth in the opening, and treats the unfinished redefinition of the second as leaving the impact incomplete.
responses.response: I agree that the Z2 classification is a real conceptual step and I kept B030 as an alternative for that reason. But the problems you name yourself bear on it: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang made the prediction that the HgTe experiment tested, Zhang is deceased, the three-dimensional work is outside the trio, and the 2016 prize already covers topological phases. A citation that tries to be fair to all of that either grows beyond three names or becomes so narrow that it names an experiment and a model rather than the concept. On the redefinition, I do not think a prize needs to wait for a decision taken by the metrology community: what the committee judges is the demonstrated and reproduced 10^-18 performance, which exists today. If you can show that the metrological uptake is genuinely in doubt, rather than delayed, I would reconsider; otherwise I would be glad to see B030 recorded as a strong later candidate.

responses.point: Lindroth defends B012 as atomic-structure physics that builds on, but does not duplicate, the comb and ion-control prizes, and holds that a second part would force an unfair one-name split from B030 or B042 under the three-person cap.
responses.response: I agree on both points, and your argument about the three-person cap is the one that settles the second-part question for me: a single-name part from B030 or B042 would be an arbitrary choice from a contested trio. In round 1 I asked whether the ion and comb lineage should be acknowledged in the citation. Having read the other files, my answer is to do that by wording rather than by names. The citation should centre on the magic-wavelength confinement of many neutral atoms, which is the part neither prior prize covers, and say nothing that sounds like a general prize for accuracy. I would resist adding a clause crediting 'earlier work' because that invites the very attribution dispute we cannot adjudicate.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, moved from B042 to B012, but concedes that B042 has the larger recent footprint and that credit around B012 has to be framed carefully against Hall and Haensch (2005) and Wineland (2012).
responses.response: Your concession about footprint is fair and I do not dispute it: B042 has produced more new physics in less time. My difficulty is that footprint is not the same as a finished discovery. The origin of the superconductivity and of the correlated states is still disputed, the experimental credit (Cao, Dean, Young and others) cannot be fitted into three names, and Olsson doubts Bistritzer's place. Those are problems that a few more years can resolve, which is why I would hold B042 for later rather than reject it. On the framing of the clock citation, I would not use the word 'precision' as the headline; the achievement is a configuration of atoms, not a number.

responses.point: Danielsson moved from B028 (ATLAS and CMS Higgs) to B012 and states a real risk that his shift reflects drift toward consensus, noting that a metrology prize sits conveniently outside his own field.
responses.response: I appreciate the candour, and I share the same caution, since I am also outside this subfield. What I would say is that the shift should rest on the attribution argument you gave, not on the absence of fundamental-theory content: B012 is the one candidate where two named people map onto two documented contributions, whereas B028 needs a rule for choosing three spokespersons among thousands, and I still cannot formulate one. If you can state such a rule I would consider B028 as a second part, but under the three-person cap that would leave only one name for B012, which I do not see as workable.

uncertainties: Whether the first-demonstration history of strontium and ytterbium lattice clocks (Takamoto, Hong, Ludlow, Lemke and others) is compatible with crediting Katori and Ye alone; I cannot verify this from the files and rely on the specialists' view.
Whether a citation worded around the magic-wavelength lattice will satisfy Eriksson's concern about novelty relative to the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
Whether the committee reads the statutes as favouring a conceptual discovery (B030) over an instrument achievement when the two are otherwise close.
Whether B042 will look settled enough, with a credit split that fits three names, if it is revisited in one or two years.
statement.conflict_note: No change. My profile documents no personal or institutional connection to Katori, Ye or any other credited name on the shortlist. My own research (turbulence, random matrices, population genetics, active matter, neural networks) is not on the shortlist, and I am not an expert in atomic clocks, so I weigh the metrology claims on the basis of the specialist members' statements.
